# Saltpetre from nitre beds (`saltpetre_production`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: helped by alkali_soda, lime_burning
- Core idea: Saltpetre (potassium nitrate) forms where dung, urine and rotting matter decay in airy, limy earth kept dry from rain: stable floors, cellars, dovecotes. A nitre bed is a roofed heap of earth, manure, straw, lime rubble and wood ash, watered with urine and turned for one to two years. The earth is then leached with water, the liquor run through wood ash (which turns the lime nitrate into true saltpetre), boiled down and skimmed, and left to cool. Saltpetre is about ten times more soluble hot than cold, so it crystallises as needles on cooling while common salt drops out during the boiling.
- Pitfalls:
  - Skipping the wood ash: the product is calcium nitrate, which draws damp and ruins gunpowder.
  - Letting rain wash the bed; nitrate is very soluble and is simply lost.
  - Expecting quick results; the bacteria need many months, warmth and air.
  - Mistaking common salt, soda or alum efflorescence for saltpetre. Appearance and taste cannot establish identity; tasting deposits risks poisoning.
- History: china: c. AD 500 – Tao Hongjing tells saltpetre from other salts by its violet flame; purified and used in alchemy, then in gunpowder by the 9th c.; india: by c. 14th c. produced from village earths; 17th–18th c. Bihar and Bengal are the world's main exporters; islamic: c. 1240 – Ibn al-Baytar calls it 'snow of China'; c. 1280 Hasan al-Rammah describes purification with wood ash; europe: late 14th c. – nitre plantations in Germany (Frankfurt 1388); 1540 Biringuccio and 1574 Ercker describe the process; 1770s French and Prussian nitre beds on a state scale; americas: from the 1830s – Chilean nitrate (sodium nitrate) from the Atacama replaces nitre beds
- Read:
  - Vannoccio Biringuccio, De la pirotechnia (1540)
  - David Cressy, Saltpeter: The Mother of Gunpowder (2013)
  - Joseph Needham et al., Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 7: Military Technology; The Gunpowder Epic (1986)
